title: Platform Operational Contracts and Oncall Playbook
author: Priya Raman
body:
Overview
--------
This page defines the Platform Operational Contract (POC) — a concise, team-facing agreement between Platform and downstream service owners that codifies ownership, SLOs, alerting expectations, degradation modes, and oncall procedures. The POC is intended to reduce ambiguity during incidents, speed cross-team coordination, and make failover and graceful degradation deterministic.

Key goals:
- Make responsibilities explicit: who fixes what and when
- Normalize SLI/SLO definitions and error budgets across critical platform services
- Provide a compact, actionable oncall runbook that any responder can follow
- Reduce blast radius by defining safe fallback behaviors and routing policies

Scope
-----
This document applies to platform-managed services listed in the Platform Critical Path (e.g., router, model-router, kv-cache, admission-queue, token-billing) and their direct dependents. It is not intended for user-land microservices not in the critical path unless explicitly referenced in a POC attachment.

Operational contract summary
---------------------------
Each POC for a service must include the following sections (convention and required fields):
1) Service metadata
   - service_name: short service id (e.g., model-router)
   - owner: team name and primary oncall (e.g., "eng-serving-runtime / oncall-model-router")
   - criticality: critical | high | medium | low
2) SLIs and SLOs (explicit metrics and aggregation windows)
   - request_success_rate (p99_for_error_free_responses) — SLO: 99.95% monthly; SLI window: 5m rolling, evaluate monthly
   - p99_latency_ms (end-to-end) — SLO: 150ms for hosted-api tier; evaluate by request-type
   - unit_cost_per_request_usd — SLO: cost drift < 10% month-over-month for steady-state workloads
3) Alerting thresholds and ownership
   - sev: mapping (sev0,sev1,sev2) with metric, threshold, and paging policy
4) Degradation policy (what happens during constrained capacity)
5) Runbook steps for common failure modes
6) Dependencies and compatible fallbacks
7) Rollout and rollback constraints (strain-tests required before canary > 20%)
8) Runbook contact and escalation
